bessel.title: An eclipse, published years in advance
bessel.mini: The total solar eclipse of 2 August 2027 is already computed to the second: six short polynomials describe the Moon's shadow on a plane through the Earth's centre. Where it falls, when, and for how long follow from a globe.
bessel.text: The total solar eclipse of 2 August 2027 crosses southern Spain, Gibraltar and North Africa, and is longest, 6 min 23.2 s, near Luxor at 10:00:21 UT [1]. None of it has been observed yet; all of it is computed. The Besselian elements describe the Moon's shadow, the wide penumbra and the narrow umbra, where it crosses a plane through the Earth's centre, perpendicular to the shadow's axis: x and y place the axis, l₁ and l₂ give the radii of the two shadows, six polynomials in time give all of them [1]. To know whether a place is in the shadow, it is projected onto that plane from its position on the Earth's surface [2]. Schematic, not to scale.
bessel.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: the 2027 eclipse arriving at published places and times that a flat map computes as well, without a globe.
nodes.title: Why there is not an eclipse every month
nodes.mini: The Moon's orbit is tilted about 5° to the Earth's. An eclipse needs a new or full moon near the line where the two orbits cross. 2027, day by day: the model finds exactly the eclipses NASA lists.
nodes.text: The Moon's orbit is tilted by 5.145° to the plane of the Earth's orbit, so most new and full moons pass above or below the Sun or the Earth's shadow. An eclipse needs one near the node line, where the two planes cross, and that line turns slowly backwards. The drawing follows 2027 day by day, with the date named above the text; sizes and distances are squeezed to fit and the tilt drawn three times too steep, as stamped. Meeus's test at each new and full moon [1] finds the annular eclipse of 6 February, the total solar eclipse of 2 August, and the lunar eclipses of 20 February, 18 July and 17 August, all in NASA's catalogue [2].
nodes.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: eclipses in 2027 that this orbital geometry fails to find, or finds on the wrong dates.
saros.title: The saros: eclipses repeat, a third of the world further west
saros.mini: After 223 lunations, 18 years 11 days and 8 hours, an eclipse returns. The extra 8 hours of the Earth's rotation put it about 111° further west each time. Three saroses later it is nearly back where it was.
saros.text: After 223 lunations, 18 years 11 days and about 8 hours, the Sun, the Moon and the node line up again almost exactly [1]. A repeating pattern says when a similar eclipse returns; it does not say where. The bands are NASA's paths of totality for three members of saros 136; the grey dots are the points of greatest eclipse of all 71 members [1]. The extra 7 h 43 min of the Earth's rotation turns each member about 111° west of the last. Three saroses later, 54 years 34 days, the extra time is 23 h 09 min, nearly a whole turn, and the series comes back close to where it was: 5.6° E in 1973, 33.2° E on 2 August 2027 [2], 53.6° E in 2081. The page computes nothing here; it only turns a globe.
saros.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: members of a saros series falling in the same place, as a flat map without rotation would have it.
local.title: The eclipse at any place, computed two ways
local.mini: The time and length of totality at one place, from NASA's elements and again from the site's own Sun and Moon. They agree to the second once the Moon is drawn at its size from there: at Luxor the observer is 6,000 km closer to it than the Earth's centre.
local.text: Local circumstances of the 2 August 2027 eclipse, by two routes, both on a globe. The first uses the published Besselian elements [1][2]. The second uses nothing from NASA: the site's own Sun and Moon, computed from an ephemeris [3], seen from that exact place, and the moment their centres come closest. The two agree on the time of maximum to a few seconds. The duration agrees only once the Moon is drawn at its size as seen from that place: near the zenith the observer is some 6,000 km closer to the Moon than the Earth's centre is, the Moon looks about 1.6% larger, and at Luxor that is worth over a minute of totality. On a plane there is no centre of the Earth to be closer to.
local.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: observed totality durations that match a Moon the same size from every place.
flat.title: The same shadow on a flat Earth, given every advantage
flat.mini: The 2027 eclipse on the flat-earth map, with its Sun and Moon lamps tuned by least squares to follow the published path. The flat shadow still stays 3,950 km from it on average, and moves the wrong way.
flat.text: A flat model on the best terms available: the usual flat map, Sun and Moon as local lamps over the real points beneath them, from the same ephemeris as the globe [2], the Moon's shadow cast along the line from the Sun lamp through the Moon. Only the ratio of the two heights moves that shadow, so it is tuned by least squares to follow NASA's published centre line [1]; the Sun's height is tuned separately. Two free parameters, both in the flat model's favour. Even so, the flat shadow stays 3,950 km from the published line on average, 8,400 km at worst, and moves 10° westward while the real shadow sweeps over 100° eastward. At the two ends its Sun stands 24° to 28° high where the real Sun is rising and setting. The time shown is named above the text; the band is bent by the map's own distortion.
flat.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: the 2 August 2027 shadow following the flat model's path rather than the published one.
lunar.title: The Earth's own shadow on the Moon
lunar.mini: In a lunar eclipse the Earth's shadow on the Moon is an arc of the same circle whether the Moon is rising, high or setting. Only a sphere casts a round shadow in every direction. Aristotle said so in the fourth century BC.
lunar.text: The oldest argument of all. Aristotle, fourth century BC: in eclipses of the Moon the outline is always curved, and since the Earth casts it, the Earth is spherical [1]. It can be sharpened. The partial phase seen at moonrise, at its highest and at moonset shows the dark edge as an arc of the same circle each time, only turned relative to the horizon. A disc casts a round shadow only when lit square on, and a straight-edged one when lit along its edge, as the last panel shows. The shadow's size is not free either: from the published sizes and distances of the Sun, Earth and Moon, the Earth's shadow at the Moon's distance is about 2.7 times the Moon's radius, as photographs show. Schematic.
lunar.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: lunar eclipses at moonrise or moonset whose shadow edge is straight or elliptical.
selen.title: The setting Sun and the eclipsed Moon, in the same sky
selen.mini: Flat-earth writers call it impossible: the Sun still up while the eclipsed Moon rises opposite. On a globe the horizon of someone on the day–night line points at both; parallax, the discs' size and the air settle it within a degree.
selen.text: A selenelion, or horizontal eclipse: the Sun and the eclipsed Moon seen together, on opposite horizons. Cleomedes reported it nearly two thousand years ago [1]; it was photographed at sunrise over Minneapolis on 8 October 2014 [2]. Top: the Sun's rays, the Earth, its shadow and the Moon at one true scale, in the plane of the Sun, the Earth's centre and the observer, who stands on the day–night line; the box enlarges the Moon's surroundings uniformly. The observer's horizon plane (dashed) points at the Sun on one side and down the shadow on the other. Bottom: the eclipsed Moon at the same instant from two places, zenith up (Adelaide in a wider field, its Moon enlarged in a box), filled with standard refraction and dashed without air; in a small frame, the Sun for each place. Seen from the surface the Moon sits about 1° lower than from the centre; half-discs and refraction give it back. From Adelaide the same Moon is high, the Sun far below the horizon, and the shadow comes from above: the “wrong side” is only the observer's up; measured from the celestial north, both places find the shadow in the same direction. The case and time are named above the text. For Brest on 31 December 2028 the totally eclipsed Moon rises in the north-east while the Sun sets in the south-west, both above a sea horizon from 16:25 to 16:33 UT; NASA lists 1 h 11 min of totality [3]. Ephemerides after Meeus [4].
selen.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: the Sun and the eclipsed Moon seen together with their upper edges adding up to more than 2° above a sea horizon, or the Moon that rises at Brest around 16:25 UT on 31 December 2028 not totally eclipsed. Or two photographs of the same eclipse, taken at the same minute in two places, showing the shadow's centre at directions from the celestial north more than 5° apart.
